name: Selective omission
statement: Selective omission is a name for material dropped from a shared account, whether by a state retelling its history or an editor choosing what to run.
meaning: The name covers two claims, and this page has to say which. In collective memory it means a group, a government or a press keeping unwelcome episodes out of the story it tells about itself. In media literacy it means a journalist leaving a fact or a whole story out. Neither sense has a research literature under this name. Memory research works on the first idea under other headings, and it has its own word for the gaps a speaker leaves in a retelling. Cuc, Koppel and Hirst called those gaps silences, and Coman, Manier and Hirst use that word for them. Media research works on the second idea as gatekeeping bias, which Spinde and colleagues also call selection bias, and as coverage bias. The term omission bias in that field is narrower than the label here suggests. Spinde and colleagues place it under spin bias and define it as dropping words from a sentence, not as dropping a story. The phrase selective omission does appear in the scholarly literature, and in other jobs. Crossref returns it as a clinical term for leaving out a test or a treatment in chosen patients, as a cartographic term for dropping features from a map as its scale shrinks, and, in a psychology journal, as the name of a training procedure run on pigeons. The entry that follows is about the label, because the label is what exists.

origin.who: Yug, an editor of the English Wikipedia
origin.note: The article Selective omission was created on 21 August 2011, and no earlier use of the phrase as the name of a bias turned up in the searches described under limits. Maintenance templates added in September 2011 flag it for thin sourcing and doubtful notability, and they are still on the page. Its definition hangs on one citation, printed as Penebaker 1997 p79-81. The source list at the foot of the same article gives page 303 of that book and spells the name Pennebaker, so the article cites two different pages for one claim. It names Routledge as the publisher, where the Internet Archive's record of the 1997 edition gives Lawrence Erlbaum Associates of Mahwah, New Jersey. That pair is not an error: Routledge sells the same book under Psychology Press with a 1997 copyright and its own ISBN.

evidence: No experiment measures selective omission. The article that names it cites two works. The first is Pennebaker, Páez and Rimé's 1997 collection on the collective memory of political events, which was not obtained here. The second is Brown and colleagues' 2009 paper in Psychological Science, and its subject is the dating of personal memories rather than omission. They collected protocols in ten cities in eight countries, between 23 and 28 people at each site, who recalled an event to each of twenty cue words and then thought aloud while dating it. In Sarajevo 24% of the justified date estimates referred to a historical period, and in Izmit 13% referred to the 1999 earthquake, six years after it. In New York City and in Ann Arbor, fewer than 1% of protocols mentioned any public event, September 11 included, and Canadians and Danes almost never mentioned one. The authors conclude that personal significance and not historical importance decides whether a public event organises autobiographical memory. Two measured literatures sit beside the label. On the memory side, what a speaker leaves out of a retelling is studied as socially shared retrieval-induced forgetting. Cuc, Koppel and Hirst had pairs study material and then had one member recall part of it while the other listened, using paired associates with 76 people, a story with 56 and free conversation with 40. Listeners later recalled less of the related material the speaker had passed over. In the first experiment that listener effect held only where listeners had been told to monitor the speaker for accuracy, and it was absent where they listened superficially. Coman, Manier and Hirst put a questionnaire about 11 September 2001 to 20 New Yorkers, sorted the answers into category sets, and then had an interviewer rehearse some answers and not others. On a later recognition test, reaction times were quicker for unpractised items from unpractised categories than for unpractised items from practised ones, t(19) = 2.30, p < .04, d = 0.56. Their second experiment replaced the interview with a free conversation of about seven minutes between 22 unrelated participants in pairs. Listeners showed the same pattern for their own memories, which the speaker had never heard, t(16) = 2.61, p < .02, d = 0.52, and speakers showed it too, t(18) = 2.63, p < .02, d = 0.56. For the speakers the omnibus test was only a trend, and the comparison reported was a planned one. Abel and Bäuml ran four experiments on the same speaker and listener design with word lists, 80 subjects in pairs in each of the first two and 96 in each of the last two. On cued recall in the first, listeners recalled 60.14% of unpractised unrelated items against 49.14% of unpractised related ones, t(39) = 2.87, p = .007, d = 0.45, and speakers 57.38% against 46.01%, t(39) = 2.58, p = .014, d = 0.41. The listener effect survived a test that controlled output order. On their old and new recognition test it was half the speaker's size and missed significance, t(47) = 1.69. On their confidence-rating test it was present and again smaller than the speaker's. On the media side, D'Alessio and Allen meta-analysed 59 quantitative studies of partisan bias in American presidential campaign coverage since 1948, yielding 132 measurements. They separate gatekeeping bias, the choice of which stories to run, from coverage bias and statement bias. Five studies allowed gatekeeping to be measured as stories per outlet per counted campaign event, and the average across them was d' = -.052, standard error .065, homogeneous and not different from zero. They report no study of gatekeeping bias in network television news. Across all three kinds of bias, all media and all elections, the grand mean was d' = -.018 weighted and -.021 unweighted, standard error .024. Their newspaper figures are the flat ones. On network television they report a small pro-Democratic tilt, at its largest 52.7% of airtime against 47.3%.

examples.tag: The anniversary that leaves out the lockout
examples.text: A town marks a century of its main employer with an exhibition covering the founding, the war work and the expansion, and not the dispute that shut the gates for a winter. Nothing on display is false. What makes it a retelling is the episode nobody chose to include.

examples.tag: The item held for a slow day
examples.text: An editor with room for four stories runs three and holds the fourth for a quiet week that never comes. No sentence in the paper is wrong, and readers cannot tell from it what was left out.

examples.tag: The family version of the quarrel
examples.text: Relatives retell a holiday to each other for years and never mention the argument that ended it. Memory research calls those gaps in a joint retelling silences, and what goes unsaid in company gets harder for everyone present to recall later.

replication.headline: Nothing has been repeated because nothing was run under this name; the nearest measured result is that details a speaker leaves out of a retelling become harder for the listener to recall, d = 0.45 among the 40 listeners in a study of 80 people tested in pairs.
replication.detail: Selective omission has no paradigm, no measure and no experiment, so there is nothing for a replication to repeat. The two literatures quoted above are cited for what they measured, and neither used the term. Socially shared retrieval-induced forgetting is the better attested of the two. Abel and Bäuml describe their first experiment as replicating prior reports of the effect on category-cued recall, and their two recall experiments give listener effects of d = 0.45 and d = 0.47 on 80 subjects each. Their two recognition experiments do not repeat that. The listener effect fell short of significance in the old and new recognition test on 96 subjects, and was smaller than the speaker's in the confidence-rating test, a contrast their abstract reports. The Coman experiments are much smaller, at 20 and 22 participants, and they report reaction times because they were after accessibility rather than loss.

limits: The label is an entry in a bias list, not a construct, and the two senses it spans do not share a method. Searches for it as a psychological or media-studies term covered Crossref, Europe PMC, English Wikipedia's List of cognitive biases and web search, and the Crossref and Wikipedia searches were re-run on 21 September 2026. Crossref's bibliographic search returns oncology, transplant surgery, colorectal surgery and road-network cartography for the phrase, along with a 1984 paper in The Psychological Record that uses it for a pigeon training procedure. A Europe PMC search for it alongside memory, recall, narrative, collective memory, media and journalism returned clinical papers about omitting treatments. The term does not appear in the List of cognitive biases. Three venues could not be re-searched on 21 September 2026. Europe PMC's REST service answered record lookups that morning and then returned 503 to every query, OpenAlex reported the free daily budget for this network's address spent, and Semantic Scholar returned 429. Google Books still returns 404 for the preview page the Wikipedia article links to. The Internet Archive copy of the Pennebaker collection is access-restricted, its search-inside route answering 403 and its text file 401. The book was not opened and nothing is quoted from it. The Routledge page for the reissue was read for publisher and copyright details only. The evidence borrowed from elsewhere carries its own limits. Cuc, Koppel and Hirst's 2007 paper, which named the silences and first showed the listener effect, was read here as the accepted manuscript marked in press, archived from the authors' host. Its figures above come from that manuscript and not from the version of record. The published article was not obtained: SAGE answers every request for it with a Cloudflare challenge, and the open copy that two indexes list is a repository record holding no file. The forgetting experiments run on pairs of strangers over minutes in a laboratory, and the listener's loss is about eleven percentage points of recall of unpractised material related to what the speaker said. Nothing in them measures a state, a newspaper or a generation. D'Alessio and Allen say plainly that gatekeeping bias is mostly unmeasurable, because the population of stories that might have been covered is unidentifiable, and that their five studies work only where campaign events could be counted. Their zero is about partisan direction summed across outlets, and they name the Washington Times, the Indianapolis Star and the Great Falls Tribune as individual papers with large biases that cancel in the aggregate. Spinde and colleagues' taxonomy of media bias, which sets out selection or gatekeeping, coverage, statement and spin bias, is an arXiv preprint and was read as the HTML of version 3. No journal version of it was found in Crossref or on arXiv on 21 September 2026.
misreadings: The first error is to read this as omission bias, no. 196, a moral-judgement effect about harm caused by inaction, which is recorded there and is a separate finding. Selective omission is about what goes missing from an account, and the shared word is doing all the work. The second error is to treat the Wikipedia article's evidence as evidence for its claim. Brown and colleagues asked people to date everyday events and found that only populations hit hard and long by a public event used it as a landmark, which says nothing about a group suppressing an unwelcome memory. The third is to read D'Alessio and Allen's zero as a finding that news outlets do not leave things out. Their result is that American newspaper campaign coverage showed no net partisan tilt, they report a small tilt on network television, and their own text calls the absolute amount of gatekeeping unknowable. The fourth is to take media research's omission bias for the thing this page is named after. In Spinde and colleagues it is a kind of spin bias and means words dropped from a sentence, and the choice of which stories to run is filed under selection bias instead. The fifth is to treat socially shared retrieval-induced forgetting as the mechanism of national forgetting. It is a laboratory effect in which one person's selective recall makes a listener's unmentioned related memories harder to reach. It did not survive one of the two recognition tests put to it. The leap from that to a textbook omitting an atrocity is a leap nobody has measured. The sixth is confusion with two entries here that describe different things. Levelling and sharpening, no. 305, is the loss of detail as a story passes down a chain of tellers, and selective amnesia, no. 274, is a clinical term for partial recall of a single episode.
